title: 2013 AMC 12A Problem 22
statement: A palindrome is a nonnegative integer number that reads the same forwards and backwards when written in base \(10\) with no leading zeros. A \(6\)-digit palindrome \(n\) is chosen uniformly at random. What is the probability that \(\dfrac{n}{11}\) is also a palindrome?

solutions.text:
Let \(m= \frac{n}{11}.\) If \(m\) had four digits, then \(n<110000,\) so the first and last digits of the six-digit palindrome \(n\) would both be \(1.\) This forces the first and last digits of the palindromic \(m\) to be \(1,\) hence \(m<2000\) and \(n<22000,\) a contradiction. Therefore \(m\) is a five-digit palindrome \(\overline{abcba}.\)

Writing \(n=11m=\overline{abcba0}+\overline{abcba},\) no carries occur exactly when \(a+b\le9\) and \(b+c\le9;\) the resulting digits are \(a,a+b,b+c,b+c,a+b,a.\) If \(a+b\ge10,\) the leading and trailing digits differ; if only \(b+c\ge10,\) the next pair differs. Thus the conditions are also necessary. The number of valid \(m\) is \[ \sum_{b=0}^{9}(10 - b)(9 - b) = 330. \]

There are \(9\cdot 10^2 = 900\) six-digit palindromes, so the probability is \(\dfrac{330}{900} = \dfrac{11}{30}.\)

Thus, the correct answer is E.
hints: The product \(11m\) is a palindrome exactly when \(a + b \le 9\) and \(b + c \le 9;\) count those
